chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Ibn Muskhan, from Yazid ibn Khalil, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who declared disassociation before the ruler from the crime of his son and his inheritance, then the son died and left wealth. Who inherits him? He said: 'His inheritance belongs to the closest of people to his father.'
ai.seo_question: Who inherits a son who was disassociated from his father in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith clarifies the inheritance status of a son in a *mula'ana* (conjugal imprecation) scenario, ruling that his share reverts to the closest paternal relative rather than the mother or other kin. It highlights the Shia juristic view that the disassociation (*tabarru'*) primarily affects the bond between father and son regarding specific liabilities, while preserving the paternal lineage's right to inheritance. This ruling is significant in distinguishing *mula'ana* from full disinheritance, ensuring the estate remains within the father's branch of the family.
